title: EXCLUSIVE: State public servants lose super in payroll policy shift
full_text:
Hundreds of public servants stand to lose thousands of dollars in superannuation contributions after controversial state government changes.
The move affects staff at the Department of Transport and Planning and the Suburban Rail Loop Authority who salary sacrifice a portion of their pay into employee benefits, such as a car lease.
It had been the government's long-standing practice to pay superannuation on pre-salary sacrifice earnings, which it did voluntarily. But last month the department abandoned the practice, costing some affected employees thousands of dollars a year.
The change was spearheaded by the Department of Government Services, which manages the payroll platform for parts of the public service, and pushed on to other departments.
In an email to staff, the Transport and Planning Department wrote that under the federal government's new Payday Super law - which compels employers to pay super every pay cycle - super contributions "must" be calculated based on earnings after salary sacrificing to employee benefits.
"As a result, the amount of earnings attracting employer superannuation contributions at 12 per cent will be lower than under the current agreement," it said.
For an employee earning $100,000 a year and salary sacrificing $500 a fortnight into a novated lease, this would decrease their annual superannuation contributions by $1560.
However, the Australian Taxation Office and independent experts said the Payday Super law did not change how salary sacrificing affected super contributions.
The ATO said the arrangement had always been voluntary and at an employer's discretion.
A Transport and Planning Department source said hundreds of employees had their entitlements cut and felt cheated by the explanation they were given.
"The Victorian government is a large and consequential employer. You would like to think that it is a model employer, that it treats its employees across the board in an equitable manner," said the source. "But this conduct is the opposite of that. It's what you expect to see from a race-to-the-bottom employer." Theo Marinis, chief economist at Coveo Partners, said he had told clients who worked for government that they generally didn't need to worry about "unscrupulous" behaviour from their employer.
"It's more the small employer you should be aware of, [but it] sounds like you should be aware of even government departments now," he said. "But I guess Victoria is in such a big mess that they're trying to scrape back some extra revenue."
A Department of Government Services spokesperson said it wanted to make sure every employee received the superannuation they were entitled to.
"We are seeking further legal advice," they said.
"If we need to make subsequent changes ... we will act."
